idiom_name: predicate function returning _Bool (C99 <stdbool.h>; bool keyword since C23)
implementation_notes: C has no user-defined conversions, so the classic structure cannot be reproduced at all: a struct cannot be tested in a condition, and the only sanctioned test is an explicit predicate such as `bool queue_is_empty(const queue_t *)` returning _Bool/bool (C99 <stdbool.h>, keyword since C23). The restriction is therefore social rather than enforced - _Bool undergoes the integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions, so `queue_is_empty(&q) + 1` still compiles. Keep the predicate call inside the condition, keep predicate results out of arithmetic, and never return 0/1/-1 from an int-typed status function that callers will compare or sum.
pitfalls: _Bool promotes to int in the usual arithmetic conversions, so nothing stops `bool empty = queue_is_empty(&q); empty + 1;` - the idiom relies on discipline and review.
Pre-C99 code and older APIs return int status (0/-1/errno); comparing those with == 1 or summing them is exactly what the pattern exists to prevent - wrap them in a predicate instead.

Before C23, `bool`, `true` and `false` are macros from <stdbool.h>, and true/false have type int rather than _Bool; code that omits the header (or redefines the macros) silently falls back to integer flags.
